---
title: "Research"
---

The question that ties my work together is **how we measure what exercise does to the
body, and what we can honestly conclude from those measurements**.

Three lines follow from it. They are not separate projects — they are the same question at
three points: how the body responds, how we measure the response, and how it adapts.

## How the body responds

Exercise-induced release of cardiac troponin (cTnT, cTnI) and NT-proBNP, with a focus on
children and adolescents, and on modelling the post-exercise kinetics rather than reading
a single time point.

The clinical stake is concrete: healthy young athletes routinely show troponin
concentrations that would suggest myocardial injury in a clinical setting. Knowing the
expected time course is what separates a normal physiological response from a finding that
warrants concern.

This line comes out of my doctoral thesis and is the most consolidated of the three.

*Main collaborators: Keith George (Liverpool John Moores University), Fred S. Apple
(University of Minnesota), Alejandro Legaz-Arrese (Universidad de Zaragoza), Luis Enrique
Carranza-García (Universidad Autónoma de Nuevo León).*

## How we measure it

Validation of field tests as alternatives to laboratory protocols: functional threshold
power, prediction of VO~2~max from short tests, an updated version of the Allen & Coggan
equation, anthropometry and muscle stiffness in road cycling.

The practical question is whether a test a coach can actually run tells you what a
laboratory test would have told you — and where it stops doing so. This is the line with
the widest applied readership.

*Main collaborators: Sebastian Sitko, Isaac López-Laval (Universidad de Zaragoza).*

## How it adapts

Strength and muscle mechanics, currently organised around **EXCURSE** — *Muscle Excursion
Range in Strength Training: Implications for Performance and Injury Prevention*
(2025–2028), which I lead together with Xavier Peirau Terès.

The earlier anchor of this line is a meta-analysis on the contralateral effects of
unilateral strength training, which remains my most cited first-author work.

This is the line I am building now, and the one with room for doctoral projects.
[More on that here](doctorat.qmd).

## The method underneath

Applied biostatistics is not a fourth line — it is how the other three are done: modelling
the time course of biological responses, Bayesian linear regression, systematic review and
meta-analysis.

It is also what explains work outside sport science. Since 2023 I have been responsible for
statistical analysis in the Clinical Neurosciences group at IRBLleida, including the
REMOTE-CAT clinical trial on prehospital remote ischaemic perconditioning in acute
ischaemic stroke.
